results.name: power_of_two_specificity
results.description: Among sets whose examples are all powers of 2 (2..64), yes rate to non-example powers of 2 minus yes rate to other even non-example targets; observed below the null means people generalise to the remaining powers of 2 less sharply (relative to evens) than the model, above means the model under-commits to the specific rule.

results.name: prev_yes_carryover
results.description: Over consecutive row pairs whose trial_index increments by 1, P(yes | previous yes) minus P(yes | previous no); observed above the null means sequential response perseveration that the trial-independent model under-produces, below means alternation.

results.name: two_example_second_minus_first
results.description: In 2-example sets with examples at least 10 apart, among non-example targets within 8 of exactly one example, yes rate near the second-presented example minus near the first; observed below the null means the model over-weights the more recent example (or under-weights the first) relative to people, above means people favour the recent example more.

results.name: outlier_cost_to_rule
results.description: Yes rate to non-example targets sharing the majority ones digit in clean sets (3-4 examples all sharing a ones digit) minus the same rate in outlier sets (all but one example share it); observed above the null means one contradicting example hurts rule-following more for people than for the model, below means people are more robust to the outlier than the model.

results.name: nearest_last_minus_nearest_first
results.description: In 3-4 example sets, among non-example targets within 10 of their nearest example, yes rate when that nearest example is the last-presented one minus when it is the first-presented one; observed below the null means the model over-produces recency (people weight the last example less than the volatile model), above means people show even stronger recency.
results.code:
# name: nearest_last_minus_nearest_first
# description: In 3-4 example sets, among non-example targets within 10 of their nearest example, yes rate when that nearest example is the last-presented one minus when it is the first-presented one; observed below the null means the model over-produces recency (people weight the last example less than the volatile model), above means people show even stronger recency.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    mat = np.full((len(uniq), 4), -1000)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        mat[i, : len(ex[s])] = ex[s]
    E = mat[codes]
    n = (E > 0).sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.abs(E - t[:, None]).astype(float)
    dist[E < 0] = 1e9
    nearest = dist.argmin(axis=1)
    dmin = dist.min(axis=1)
    base = (n >= 3) & (dmin > 0) & (dmin <= 10)
    a = base & (nearest == n - 1)
    b = base & (nearest == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_position_rule_contrast
results.description: In 3-4 example sets with one ones-digit outlier, yes rate to non-example majority-digit targets when the outlier is in the second half of the presented order minus when it is in the first half; the volatile model predicts a late outlier hurts the rule more (negative), so observed above the null means people show less recency (order matters less) than the model, below means more.
results.code:
# name: outlier_position_rule_contrast
# description: In 3-4 example sets with one ones-digit outlier, yes rate to non-example majority-digit targets when the outlier is in the second half of the presented order minus when it is in the first half; the volatile model predicts a late outlier hurts the rule more (negative), so observed above the null means people show less recency (order matters less) than the model, below means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    late, dg = {}, {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        e = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        late[s], dg[s] = -1, -1
        if len(e) >= 3:
            vals, cnt = np.unique([x % 10 for x in e], return_counts=True)
            if cnt.max() == len(e) - 1:
                mm = int(vals[cnt.argmax()])
                pos = [i for i, x in enumerate(e) if x % 10 != mm][0]
                late[s] = int(pos >= len(e) / 2.0)
                dg[s] = mm
    lt = sets.map(late).to_numpy()
    m = sets.map(dg).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    is_ex = np.array([str(x) in s.split(",") for x, s in zip(t, sets)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    rule = (t % 10 == m) & ~is_ex & (lt >= 0)
    a, b = rule & (lt == 1), rule & (lt == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: clean_digit_rule_vs_range
results.description: In 3-4 example sets whose examples all share a ones digit, yes rate to same-ones-digit targets outside the examples' min-max hull minus yes rate to other-digit targets inside the hull; observed above the null means people let the digit rule dominate the range more than the model, below means the model over-weights the rule relative to the range.
results.code:
# name: clean_digit_rule_vs_range
# description: In 3-4 example sets whose examples all share a ones digit, yes rate to same-ones-digit targets outside the examples' min-max hull minus yes rate to other-digit targets inside the hull; observed above the null means people let the digit rule dominate the range more than the model, below means the model over-weights the rule relative to the range.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    lo, hi, dg = {}, {}, {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        e = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        lo[s], hi[s], dg[s] = min(e), max(e), -1
        if len(e) >= 3 and len(set(x % 10 for x in e)) == 1:
            dg[s] = e[0] % 10
    L = sets.map(lo).to_numpy()
    H = sets.map(hi).to_numpy()
    m = sets.map(dg).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    clean = m >= 0
    inside = (t > L) & (t < H)
    outside = (t < L) | (t > H)
    a = clean & outside & (t % 10 == m)
    b = clean & inside & (t % 10 != m)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_neighbourhood_yes_rate
results.description: In sets of 3-4 examples where all but one share a ones digit (one "outlier" example), the yes rate to non-example targets within 5 of the outlier that do not share the majority ones digit; observed above the null means people generalise around a rule-violating example more than the model (which treats it as noise / a brief switch), below means less.
